newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. demands threaten to soften global landmine ban.
newsitem.headline: U.S. demands threaten to soften global landmine ban.

text.p: U.S. insistence that its own "smart" anti-personnel landmines be exempt from Canada's proposed global ban on the weapons could water down the Canadian initiative, military analysts say.

"Clearly it's going to take some real negotiation," Canada's Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy told Reuters late on Monday after U.S. President Bill Clinton announced he had decided to support Canada's landmines initiative.

Axworthy is the driving force behind the "Ottawa process" -- a Canadian-led effort to forge a worldwide ban on the use, export, production and stockpiling of anti-personnel landmines. Representatives from more than 100 countries will gather in Oslo in two weeks to draft a treaty to be signed in Ottawa in December.

Canada and most other supporters of the ban want a total, unambiguous prohibition of landmines. But the United States, which reversed itself and decided to throw its weight behind the process on Monday after cold shouldering the plan since January, is demanding several important exemptions.
Under pressure from the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Washington has insisted its "smart" or self-destructing mines should be exempted from the ban.

The United States also wants to keep landmines in use in the demilitarized zone between North and South Korea. And it has proposed delaying the enforcement of any treaty until Russia, China and 75 percent of the world's landmine users and producers sign on.

The demands "probably kill" Axworthy's chances of pushing through a worldwide ban with no exceptions, said military analyst Jim Hansen, a spokesman for the Canadian Institute of Strategic Studies in Toronto.
While there is a chance that tensions between North and South Korea will ease before December, there is little hope that Russia and China will sign on to the Ottawa process by then, Hansen said.

Anti-personnel mines, designed to maim, claim a new victim every 22 minutes. Most of the victims are women and children in war-torn areas. Canadian officials say there are about 100 million buried landmines in the world.
Russia and China, the world's largest producers of landmines, could use Clinton's request to keep "smart" mines in use as a reason not to join the process, Hansen said.

"The Russians and Chinese are probably delighted because they can use this as an excuse not to sign on," Hansen said. Axworthy "has got a bit of a problem. He'll have to do a bit of tap-dancing there."
The Canadian foreign minister, however, seems prepared to tap dance.
"It's going to be a very interesting few months," he told Reuters in a telephone interview. "It's the last 100 metres to the wire that's always the toughest."

Axworthy noted the United States has the power to influence landmine policy in key countries like Russia, China and Japan. And he believes the American demands are merely an opening gambit, with overall U.S. support for the Ottawa process being far more important than Washington's demands for changes.

"(The Americans) now want to be part of the Ottawa process, so they'll have to put their ideas on the table," Axworthy said. "It's not just us alone" demanding a clear and total ban on landmines, he added.

While the American demands threaten to soften any treaty, the United States is not immune to pressure from a united front of other countries, said John English, Canada's special representative for landmines.
"What we've said all along is no exceptions," English told Reuters. "These exceptions are definitely too many. I think it will lead to a common front (against the United States)."
Clinton will also have to pay attention to strong domestic public opinion in favor of a clear and total landmines ban, analysts said.
